nodes.description: APOBEC-family cytidine deaminase activity contributes a separate footprint carrying the APOBEC substitution signatures. Its regional behaviour links it to structural catastrophe rather than to replication timing: APOBEC-signature mutations cluster around complex structural-variant breakpoints, consistent with single-stranded DNA exposed during chromothripsis being edited by the deaminase. Clonality analysis places APOBEC mutations early in tumor evolution while the impaired-recombination signatures accompanying this footprint appear subclonally, which is the argument for reading APOBEC editing as the driving aetiology here and the recombination signatures as a later, separate process.

nodes.description: Androgen receptor binding is a mutagenic event and not only a transcriptional one. Whole-genome analysis of the Pan Prostate Cancer Group cohort identifies AR-mediated mutagenesis as the most recurrent integrated mutational footprint in chromosomally unstable primary tumors, raising the local mutation rate at tumor-specific AR binding sites (TARBSs) and concentrating chromoplexy - chains of interchromosomal complex rearrangements - specifically and uniquely at those sites. Chromoplexy is an established generator of ERG fusions, and it is concentrated at AR binding sites, so this process is the most likely origin of the androgen-driven fusion events this entry already models - but the step that AR binding is what localizes the chromoplexy remains an inference from co-localization, not a demonstrated one. Its intensity tracks the epigenetic state of the site rather than AR occupancy alone: TARBSs are enriched for unmethylated CpGs, which places the process in early-replicating, transcriptionally active chromatin and accounts for the local depletion of the 5-methylcytosine-deamination signature SBS1 there.

nodes.description: A second impaired-homologous-recombination footprint is separable from the canonical BRCA-driven one by both its driver and its damage pattern. It is associated with CDK12 mutation, which phenocopies impaired homologous recombination without BRCA1/2 loss, and its structural signature is dominated by tandem duplications rather than by microhomology-mediated deletion. It is enriched in patients of African ancestry and confers a high risk of progression to metastasis. Curating it separately matters clinically, because a tumor can carry a homologous-recombination-like footprint while being negative for the BRCA alterations that current PARP-inhibitor eligibility is written around.

nodes.description: Loss of DNA mismatch repair, most often through MSH2 alteration, produces the replicative-slippage footprint that combines the MMR-associated substitution signatures with the characteristic indel signature, and yields microsatellite instability. Its topographical behaviour is diagnostic: where the other mutational processes are strongly biased by replication timing and chromatin state, mismatch-repair-deficient tumors mutate at a near-uniform rate across the genome, consistent with replication-coupled repair normally being most efficient in early-replicating regions. Unlike the other footprints curated here it is also detectable in chromosomally stable tumors. This is the mechanism behind the entry's biomarker-selected checkpoint-blockade indication.

nodes.description: A distinct integrated footprint attributes part of the mutation burden to oxidative DNA damage handled by a faulty base-excision repair pathway, marked by the substitution signature SBS18 and concentrated in late-replicating regions. It is anti-correlated with tumor hypoxia score, so it reads as an oxygen-dependent damage process rather than as a consequence of the hypoxic niche. Among the footprints that carry prognostic weight, this is one of the four associated with shorter time to metastasis, which makes oxidative mutagenesis a candidate risk axis independent of Gleason grade group and tumor mutational burden.

nodes.description: Dysfunctional DNA replication is the dominant mutational process in roughly a quarter of chromosomally unstable primary prostate cancers, resolving into two integrated footprints: one combining mitotic-machinery defects with replication stress, and one linked to SPOP and WNT-pathway alterations. Faulty replicated DNA persisting into mitosis yields copy-number and complex structural change rather than a distinctive base-substitution spectrum, which is why the process was only resolved by integrating substitution, indel, copy-number and complex structural-variant signatures. Clinically this footprint separates from the metastasis-associated processes in two ways: it predominates in late-onset disease, and higher activity of the SPOP-associated footprint marked tumors that failed later on AR pathway inhibitors than on taxanes.
